patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Jackson is a 38-year-old Black male personal trainer with no significant past medical history who was brought by friends from a social gathering after he developed a sudden catastrophic headache. His friends report that he had been using cocaine approximately 30-45 minutes prior to the onset. He suddenly grabbed his head and screamed, then had a brief loss of consciousness lasting approximately one minute. He regained consciousness before EMS arrival. He is now alert and oriented but in severe pain with a 10/10 headache, vomiting, and marked neck stiffness. He has no prior history of headaches. He denies any other drug use. He is otherwise healthy. The relationship between cocaine use and aneurysmal SAH is well-established: cocaine causes catecholamine surges with acute severe hypertension that can rupture pre-existing cerebral aneurysms. His blood pressure on arrival is severely elevated. Cocaine causes sympathomimetic crisis, vasoconstriction, and hypertension — the acute BP surge is the precipitant. He is a non-smoker and non-drinker with no medical history but the cocaine use is the single most important risk factor in this case. The brief LOC at onset is consistent with a large SAH causing transient ICP elevation.

results.finding: Cocaine increases SAH risk 5-28 fold through catecholamine surge and acute hypertension
Pre-existing aneurysm is typical - cocaine is the precipitant not the cause of aneurysm formation
BP management in cocaine SAH: avoid labetalol (minimal alpha blockade) - use phentolamine or nicardipine
Avoid pure beta-blockers in cocaine toxidrome - paradoxical hypertension from unopposed alpha stimulation
Addiction counseling and cessation essential after recovery

output.summary: Cocaine is associated with a substantially elevated risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage, attributed to catecholamine-mediated acute hypertensive surges that may precipitate rupture of a pre-existing intracranial aneurysm. Pharmacological management of acute cocaine-related hypertension favors agents with combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic blockade or calcium channel blockade; pure beta-adrenergic blockade may result in unopposed alpha stimulation and paradoxical worsening of hypertension. Standard evidence-based management of aneurysmal SAH applies once the acute hypertensive crisis is treated. Clinical correlation recommended.
